questions.prompt: Pre-training on one 1,000-token document. How many next-token training examples does it give?
questions.why: Every position except the last predicts the token after it: n − 1 = 999. The model makes all 999 predictions in one forward pass: the vector at position i predicts token i + 1.

questions.prompt: Why does pre-training need no human labels?
options: The text supplies the answer: the right label at each position is simply the next token
A smaller model labels the text first, and the large model then learns from those labels
Labels are added later during fine-tuning; pre-training only learns word statistics
It does need labels; they are crowdsourced, which is why pre-training costs so much
questions.why: Self-supervised learning: the data is its own label. That is why pre-training can use trillions of tokens of raw text.

questions.prompt: Loss = −ln p(correct token). The model gives the correct token 50%. What is the loss?
Same formula, but the model gives the correct token only 1%. What is the loss?
questions.why: −ln 0.01 = ln 100 ≈ 4.6. Dropping from 50% to 1% multiplies the loss by about 6.6, while 1 − p would only go from 0.5 to 0.99.

questions.prompt: Why use −ln p instead of 1 − p as the loss?
options: −ln p grows without limit as p → 0, so confident wrong answers are punished hard; 1 − p caps the penalty at 1
1 − p can go negative when the model is very confident, which would reward a wrong answer instead of punishing it
−ln p is cheaper to compute on a GPU than a subtraction across the whole vocabulary
There is no difference in what the model learns: both are lowest at p = 1, so −ln p is just convention
questions.why: Being 1% sure of the right answer should hurt far more than being 50% sure. The log makes the penalty grow sharply as p shrinks, and it pairs with softmax into a simple gradient (p − 1 on the right token).

questions.prompt: With softmax and cross-entropy, what is the gradient on each logit?
options: p − 1 for the correct token, and p for every other token
1 for the correct token, 0 for every other token
−ln p for the correct token, and 0 for every other token
p for the correct token, and p − 1 for every other token
questions.why: Push the right answer up (p − 1 is negative, so gradient descent raises it) and push every other token down in proportion to how much probability it took.

questions.prompt: What would the model learn if you trained without the causal mask?
options: To copy the next token from the input, since it could see it; at generation that token doesn't exist yet
Exactly the same thing, only slower, since each position would also attend to positions it then ignores
To generate whole sentences at once, since every position would see every other one at the same time
Nothing: training would crash, because softmax needs at least one masked score in every row
questions.why: Without the mask, position i can attend to token i + 1, which is its own answer. The loss drops fast by cheating. At generation the future isn't there, so the model has learned nothing useful.

questions.prompt: How is the causal mask applied in code?
options: Add −∞ to scores above the diagonal before softmax, so future positions get exactly 0 weight
Delete the future tokens from the input, so each position runs on a shorter sequence
Multiply the values of future tokens by 0.5, so they count for half in the weighted average
Set the attention weights above the diagonal to 0 after the weighted average has been taken
questions.why: scores + mask, where the mask is 0 on and below the diagonal and −∞ above it. e^−∞ = 0, so the future gets exactly zero share and the remaining shares still sum to 1.

questions.prompt: Training runs all positions in parallel; generation runs one at a time. Why do the two compute the same thing?
options: The mask makes each position see only itself and earlier positions, exactly as during generation
Generation quietly retrains the model after each token so it stays in step with training
They don't match exactly; a short extra training phase adjusts the model so generation roughly agrees
Both run at the same temperature, so the probabilities they compute come out identical
questions.why: In both cases position i depends only on tokens 1…i. That is also why the KV cache (Lesson 2) and prompt caching are correct.

questions.prompt: Training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. A 70B model on 15 trillion tokens. How many operations, in units of 10²⁴?
questions.why: 6 × 70 × 10⁹ × 15 × 10¹² = 6,300 × 10²¹ = 6.3 × 10²⁴. The 6 is 2 for the forward pass plus about 4 for the backward pass.

questions.prompt: Run those 6.3 × 10²⁴ operations on 8,192 GPUs at 989 trillion operations per second each, with 40% utilization. How many days?
Which are real differences between training and serving infrastructure? Pick all that apply.
options: Training GPUs must exchange gradients every step, so the network and stragglers matter as much as the chips
Training needs several times the memory per parameter (gradients and optimizer state)
One failed GPU stalls a whole synchronized training job, so teams checkpoint often
Serving updates the weights after every request
Training uses a KV cache to skip recomputation
questions.why: Training is one huge synchronized job that writes weights; serving is many independent requests that only read them. Serving never updates weights, and the KV cache is a generation-time trick.

questions.prompt: You ask a base model (pre-training only) “What is a river bank?” What is it most likely to do?
options: Continue the text as a document would, perhaps with more quiz questions, rather than answer
Answer politely like a chat assistant, since question-and-answer text is all over its training data
Refuse, because a base model has no instructions telling it how to respond to users
Return an error, since the prompt lacks the chat template a base model expects
questions.why: A base model only continues text. Answering as an assistant is learned in post-training.

questions.prompt: What does a chat template do?
options: Wraps each turn in special tokens like <|user|> and flattens the messages into one string to continue
Adds a second, smaller model that tracks the conversation and hands the main model one turn at a time
Stores past conversations on the server so the model can recall them in a later session
Rewrites the user's prompt into a fixed question format, the one the base model saw most in pre-training
questions.why: The API's messages become one sequence; the server appends the assistant header, and the model continues until it emits the end-of-turn token. The model is still predicting the next token.

questions.prompt: Base model vs chat model after supervised fine-tuning (SFT): what changes?
options: Only the weight values, via more training with the same next-token loss on curated prompt → answer pairs
A new answer-generation layer is added on top of the base model, and only that layer is trained on dialogue
The tokenizer is retrained for dialogue, so turns and roles get pieces of their own
The next-token loss is replaced by a reward score, so the model learns what people prefer
questions.why: SFT is the same forward pass, the same −ln p per position, the same gradient. Only the data changes, plus a per-token weight that decides which positions are scored.

questions.prompt: SFT scores only the answer tokens (weight 0 on the template and prompt). What would go wrong if it scored the prompt too?
options: Effort would go into predicting user messages, so the model learns to write prompts as well as answers
Nothing much; scoring the prompt only costs a little more compute per training example
The causal mask would stop working, because the prompt tokens would then be able to see the answer after them
The model would forget its vocabulary, since prompt tokens would dominate every gradient step
questions.why: The goal is to learn how to respond. Scoring the prompt teaches the model to imitate users, and wastes the small SFT dataset on text it doesn't need to produce.

questions.prompt: Llama 2 used about 27,540 written SFT examples versus about 2 trillion pre-training tokens. What does that say?
options: Knowledge comes from pre-training; a small, high-quality SFT set mainly shapes behavior and format
SFT examples teach facts far more efficiently than pre-training tokens, so most knowledge comes from SFT
Pre-training is mostly wasted, since the useful skills only appear once SFT begins
SFT overwrites most of what pre-training learned, so a small set is enough to rebuild it
questions.why: Post-training is tiny next to pre-training, yet it decides how the model behaves: it steers what the base model already knows rather than teaching new knowledge.

questions.prompt: RLHF vs DPO: what does each need?
options: RLHF: a reward model and reinforcement learning, generating during training. DPO: one loss on chosen/rejected pairs
RLHF: only human-written answers, trained like SFT. DPO: a reward model scoring the model's own answers
Both need a trained reward model and sampled answers during training; DPO just trains its reward model faster
RLHF trains on single answers rated by people; DPO needs whole conversations, with every turn scored by people
questions.why: Both learn from preference pairs. DPO skips the reward model and the reinforcement-learning loop, which is why it spread quickly: simpler, cheaper, and stable.

questions.prompt: The DPO loss is −ln σ(gap). What is the “gap”?
options: How much more the model now favors chosen over rejected, compared with the starting model
The difference in length between the chosen and rejected answers, which DPO penalizes
The reward model's score for the chosen answer minus its score for the rejected one, as in RLHF
The number of tokens at which the chosen and rejected answers differ from each other
questions.why: Measured relative to the starting model, so the model is pushed toward the chosen answer without drifting far from what it was.

questions.prompt: TTFT is 0.3 s and TPOT is 25 ms. How many seconds until a 401-token answer has fully arrived?
questions.why: The first token arrives at TTFT; the other 400 each take one TPOT: 0.3 + 400 × 0.025 = 0.3 + 10 = 10.3 s.

questions.prompt: In a chat app, which latency does a user notice first?
options: TTFT (time to first token): how long before anything appears
End-to-end latency: the time until the whole answer has finished
Throughput: total tokens per second across all users
Time to compute the KV cache size
questions.why: With streaming, the wait before the first token is the felt delay; after that, a TPOT faster than reading speed feels smooth.

questions.prompt: Prefill floor: 2 operations per parameter per token. A 70B model on GPUs delivering 1,978 trillion operations per second in total. Minimum TTFT for a 2,000-token prompt, in milliseconds?
questions.why: 2 × 70 × 10⁹ = 140 billion per token ÷ 1,978 × 10¹² ≈ 71 µs per token. × 2,000 ≈ 142 ms, before queueing and overheads.

questions.prompt: You raise the decode batch from 1 to 64. What happens?
options: Total tokens per second rise a lot, each user's TPOT rises a little, and KV memory caps how many users fit
Both total throughput and each user's TPOT improve, since the GPU is busier and works more efficiently per token
Total throughput stays the same, since the GPU is already busy; each user just gets 64 times slower
Each user's TPOT stays exactly the same until compute runs out, and throughput rises 64 times
questions.why: Tick = (weight bytes + B × cache bytes per user) ÷ bandwidth. At small B the weight read dominates and is shared, so extra users are nearly free. Cache reads grow with B, and cache memory runs out first.

questions.prompt: Toy server: 16 GB of weights, 1 GB of KV cache per user, 1 TB/s of memory bandwidth. Tick = (16 + B × 1) GB ÷ 1 TB/s. With B = 16 users, how many tokens per second in total?
questions.why: Tick = 32 GB ÷ 1,000 GB/s = 32 ms, one token per user per tick: 16 ÷ 0.032 = 500 tokens/s. With one user: 17 ms → about 59 tokens/s. Sixteen users get 8.5× the throughput for under 2× the TPOT.

questions.prompt: Which backend pattern is decode batching most like?
options: Group commit: many transactions share one disk flush, so each waits a bit longer but throughput rises
A circuit breaker: requests beyond the batch size are rejected until the GPU recovers
Read replicas: each user in the batch gets a copy of the weights to read from in parallel
A CDN edge cache: answers to common prompts are stored near users and served without running the model
questions.why: The expensive shared step (reading every weight; flushing the log) is paid once per batch instead of once per request.

questions.prompt: Why does an output token cost more GPU time than an input token?
options: Input tokens share each weight read in prefill; each output step reads all the weights to emit one token per user
Output tokens pass through more layers than input tokens, since the model must also pick the next token
Output tokens are longer than input tokens, because the model writes whole words rather than pieces
Providers charge more for output to discourage long answers; the GPU time per token is actually about the same
questions.why: Prefill is compute-bound and shares each weight read across the whole prompt. Decode is memory-bound: a full read of weights plus caches per tick. The price gap mirrors that GPU-time gap.

questions.prompt: When would the cost gap between output and input tokens shrink? Pick all that apply.
options: Larger decode batches, so each weight read is shared by more users
Smaller KV caches (shorter contexts, fewer KV heads), so more users fit in a batch
Quantized weights, so each tick reads fewer bytes
Longer contexts per request
Higher temperature
questions.why: Anything that spreads or shrinks the bytes read per tick helps decode. Longer contexts make output pricier (bigger caches to read every tick); temperature doesn't change the work.

questions.prompt: An H100 does about 989 trillion operations per second and reads about 3.35 trillion bytes per second. How many operations can it do per byte read before memory stops being the bottleneck?
questions.why: 989 ÷ 3.35 ≈ 295. Decode at 16-bit does about 1 operation per weight byte per user, so it would take ~295 users to become math-bound, and KV memory runs out long before.

questions.prompt: Two GPUs at $4 per GPU-hour produce 1,000 output tokens per second. What is the cost per million output tokens, in dollars?
questions.why: $8 per hour ÷ 3.6 million tokens per hour (1,000 × 3,600) ≈ $2.22 per million.

questions.prompt: Same setup ($8 per hour, 1,000 tokens/s while busy), but the GPUs are busy only half the time. Cost per million output tokens, in dollars?
questions.why: You pay for the whole hour but produce only 1.8 million tokens: $8 ÷ 1.8 ≈ $4.44. Halving utilization doubles the cost per token.

questions.prompt: Which levers lower cost per million tokens? Pick all that apply.
options: More tokens per second while busy (batching, quantization, better kernels)
A higher busy share of each paid hour (traffic, autoscaling, sharing GPUs across models)
Lower temperature
A bigger vocabulary
questions.why: Cost per token = dollars per hour ÷ tokens per hour. Only throughput-while-busy and utilization move that ratio.

questions.prompt: Why is it safe to reuse a stored KV prefix for a different request?
options: Keys and values at position i depend only on tokens 1…i, so an identical prefix always gives identical KV
KV values come from the weights alone, so they are the same for every prompt and any stored copy works for any request
The server re-checks every stored value against the new request and recomputes any that differ
It isn't fully safe; small errors from a different request's context are accepted for the speed
questions.why: The causal mask makes the prefix's KV independent of whatever comes after it. Exact token match is required: one different early token changes everything after it.

questions.prompt: An app sends a 3,000-token system prompt plus a short user message. How should it order the prompt to keep prompt-cache hits?
options: Fixed content first (system prompt, tools, examples); changing content (user message, time) last
User message first, so it gets the most attention, then the system prompt and tools after it
Put a timestamp at the top so the cache can tell how old the prompt is and expire it in time
Order doesn't matter; the cache matches any shared stretch of text wherever it appears in the prompt
questions.why: The cache matches prefixes. Anything that varies near the start breaks the match for everything after it.

questions.prompt: On a cache hit for that 3,000-token prefix, what improves? Pick all that apply.
options: TTFT: only the new tokens need prefill
Input cost: providers bill cached input tokens at a discount
TPOT: each output token gets much faster
The answer gets more accurate
questions.why: Prompt caching skips prefill work, which is TTFT and input cost. Decode still reads the same weights and the same (now longer) cache each tick, and the output is identical.

questions.prompt: Which backend pattern is prompt caching most like?
options: A content-addressed cache with a TTL: hash prefix blocks, look them up, expire after minutes
A write-through cache in front of a database: every new prompt is written to the cache and to disk
A message queue: prompts wait until enough with the same prefix arrive to process them together
Database sharding: each prefix is pinned to one server, which keeps its cache forever
questions.why: Servers hash fixed-size blocks of the prefix and look them up; entries hold GPU or host memory, so they expire. Same key, same content, safe to share.

questions.prompt: A 70B model's weights at 8-bit (1 byte each). How many GB?
questions.why: 70 billion × 1 byte = 70 GB, half of the 140 GB at 16-bit. Decode reads every weight each tick, so the tick's weight read halves too.

questions.prompt: Quantization speeds up decode a lot but prefill much less. Why?
options: Decode is memory-bound, so fewer weight bytes speed it up; prefill is compute-bound, so smaller weights barely help
Prefill doesn't read the weights at all; it only builds the KV cache from the prompt's embeddings
Quantization only shrinks the output layer, which decode runs on every step but prefill runs only once per prompt
Prefill results are already cached from earlier requests, so there is little left for it to speed up
questions.why: Speed follows the bottleneck. Decode waits on memory; prefill waits on math. Lower-precision math units (e.g. FP8 tensor cores at 2× BF16) are what make prefill faster too.

questions.prompt: Quantizing weights to 8-bit gives decode “two multiplying wins”. What are they?
options: Each tick reads half the weight bytes, and the freed memory holds more KV caches for a bigger batch
The model needs fewer layers and a smaller vocabulary, so each decode tick has less work to do in total
Prompts and answers get shorter, since 8-bit weights produce more compact tokens
Temperature can drop and sampling can be skipped, since 8-bit logits are already sharp
questions.why: Faster ticks times more users per tick. The cost is some quality, depending on the method and the bit width.

questions.prompt: A 70B model on 2 H100s at 16-bit misses its TPOT target and fits only a few users. Which fix keeps quality but adds communication overhead and a bigger minimum deployment?
options: Adding GPUs (tensor parallelism): more bandwidth per tick and more room for caches
Quantizing to 8-bit: half the bytes per tick and room for twice the caches
Raising the batch size: more users share each weight read, so each user's TPOT drops
Lowering the temperature: fewer candidate tokens per step, so each tick is faster
questions.why: Splitting weights and caches across more GPUs halves the bytes each one reads, but they must talk every layer and the bill grows with them. Quantization keeps the GPU count but can cost quality; a bigger batch makes TPOT worse, not better.

questions.prompt: Decode floor: each tick reads all the weights. 140 GB of weights, 6.7 TB/s of combined bandwidth. Minimum TPOT in milliseconds (ignore the cache reads)?
questions.why: 140 GB ÷ 6,700 GB/s ≈ 0.0209 s ≈ 21 ms per token, before cache reads and overheads.

questions.prompt: Which backend idea is the causal mask most like?
options: A snapshot read: each transaction sees only what committed before it, never later writes
A load balancer: each token is routed only to the attention heads that are free
Rate limiting: each token may only attend to a fixed number of others per step
A dead-letter queue: future tokens are parked to one side and processed after the current one finishes
questions.why: Each position sees only earlier positions, the way a snapshot sees only earlier commits. That one-way visibility is what makes caching the past safe.
